explanation: Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi had begun uniting Japan before him. Ieyasu and his heirs ruled as shoguns from 1603 to 1867, more than 250 largely peaceful years.

The Tokugawa shogunate ruled Japan until 1867.
Oda Nobunaga died in 1582 and Toyotomi Hideyoshi in 1598, before Sekigahara; Minamoto no Yoritomo founded the first shogunate in the 1190s.
Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi began the unification of Japan before Ieyasu.
The Tokugawa shoguns ruled from 1603 to 1867, a largely peaceful period of more than 250 years.

evidence.query: Tokugawa Ieyasu won Battle of Sekigahara 1600, became shogun 1603, Tokugawa shogunate lasted until 1867; Oda Nobunaga died 1582; Toyotomi Hideyoshi died 1598
evidence.summaryExcerpt: Sekigahara (1600): Sources date the battle to October 21, 1600, and describe Ieyasu's victory there as establishing his control over Japan. One source puts it this way: In 1600 Ieyasu's forces triumphed at the decisive Battle of Sekigahara, making him the undisputed master of Japan. Shogun (1603): Emperor Go-Yōzei conferred the title in 1603. Ieyasu resigned two years later in favor of his son Hidetada, but maintained power.

claimResults.note: Sekigahara on 21 October 1600; Emperor Go-Yozei made Ieyasu shogun in 1603.

evidence.query: Tokugawa Ieyasu won Battle of Sekigahara 1600, became shogun 1603, Tokugawa shogunate lasted until 1867; Oda Nobunaga died 1582; Toyotomi Hideyoshi died 1598
evidence.summaryExcerpt: Your query's claims are well supported. The one wrinkle is the end date: sources differ between 1867 and 1868. End of the shogunate: Dates vary. Britannica's Japan-focused sources say In 1867 the Tokugawa government fell, imperial rule was reestablished, and a Britannica student article gives it was in power from 1603 until 1867. Wikipedia's Tokugawa shogunate article dates the military government to 1603 to 1868, and the last shogun's term is listed as 1866–1867. The 1867 date marks the last shogun's resignation, and 1868 marks the formal end of the bakufu under the Meiji Restoration.

claimResults.note: Checker B's 1867 or 1868 note: Britannica dates Tokugawa rule from 1603 until 1867, and the summary explains that 1867 marks the last shogun's resignation and 1868 the formal end of the bakufu under the Meiji Restoration. The claim matches the resignation and a current reference work, so the two dates mark different events rather than conflicting; 'until 1867, when the last shogun resigned' would remove any doubt.

evidence.query: Minamoto no Yoritomo appointed shogun 1192 founded Kamakura shogunate first shogunate; Edo period more than 250 years of peace Pax Tokugawa
evidence.summaryExcerpt: Kamakura shogunate (1192): Minamoto no Yoritomo's 1192 appointment is well documented, though sources differ on the start date. One source notes that in the past, the most popular theory was that the year was 1192, when Minamoto no Yoritomo was appointed Seii Taishōgun. ... Some scholars note that Japanese history textbooks as of 2016 do not specify a specific year for the beginning of the Kamakura period. Yoritomo's government in Kamakura is described as the first military government in which the shogun with the samurai were the de facto rulers of Japan.

claimResults.note: Nobunaga's death (21 June 1582) and Hideyoshi's (18 September 1598) are confirmed in search 23, and Yoritomo's government in Kamakura is the first military government. But the founding date is contested: the summary says 1192, his appointment as shogun, was the most popular theory in the past, and that Japanese textbooks as of 2016 give no single year. So 'founded the first shogunate in the 1190s' fails as written.

evidence.query: Minamoto no Yoritomo appointed shogun 1192 founded Kamakura shogunate first shogunate; Edo period more than 250 years of peace Pax Tokugawa
evidence.summaryExcerpt: Edo period and Pax Tokugawa: The Tokugawa shogunate's peace is widely described as a stable period, though not as a "250 years" figure. One source calls it a forced peace that was maintained through a variety of measures that weakened the daimyōs and ensured their loyalty to the shōgunate. Britannica says the Tokugawa ruled for 265 years. Another describes the period as a time of internal peace, political stability, and economic growth. Caveat: The 1603–1867 dates are standard, and the 265-year rule figure matches them. The "more than 250 years" claim is consistent with that span, but I found no source that uses that exact wording.

claimResults.note: Britannica: the Tokugawa ruled for 265 years, a period described as one of internal peace and political stability (a 'forced peace' in one source's words). 1603 to 1867 is 264 years by subtraction, so 'more than 250 years' holds; the summary notes only that no source uses that exact wording.
